day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: On it. Let me grab what I can before something catches fire.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah, honestly. It's like your brain just shuts off for a second. But we made it, so let's focus on that. Are you hurt anywhere?

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey, I get it. Take a minute. But we're going to need you when you're ready, okay? No pressure right now, just breathe.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Okay, so water is the priority then. Three days of first aid is actually decent. Is there anything we can use to collect rainwater? And food — are we near any kind of tree line or vegetation? We need to figure out what's around us before it gets dark.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Agreed. Signal should probably be third for now since we don't even know if anyone's tracking our flight path yet. Water first — DaVinci, can you start on something to collect rainwater while Donatello and I check out that tree line? Michelangelo, if you're feeling up to it, staying here and keeping an eye on the supplies would actually be really helpful. We need someone we trust watching everything.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Michelangelo gets one, no question. The rest of us can figure it out — sit close to the fire, share the other one, whatever. It's one night.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Michelangelo — someone needs to hold down camp and honestly those two are better together anyway. What do I need to know about the route?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Wait, I thought I was going to handle the water run? I already said I'd go. If you're switching that up, fine, but let's not have two plans going at once — that's how things fall through the cracks. I'll take the first-aid kit since I actually want to know what we're working with. DaVinci can handle patching the camp.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
Yeah, I have it — I've been sorting through the kit. Come here, what do you need it for, are you hurt?

Also, hey — I saw what you did with the bottle. That was a good call. We're going to need to talk to Donatello about that.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Okay, that's two incidents now. The drink and the crackers. I'm not going to let that slide — we literally have a rationing plan sitting right there in the middle of camp that she wrote herself. That's not just selfish, that's hypocritical.

I get that you're worried about making things worse, but honestly? Not saying anything is worse. If she keeps doing this we're going to run out of resources way faster than we should. We need to address it directly and calmly, no drama, just facts. You and me, together, when she gets back. You don't have to do the talking if you don't want to, I'll handle it. But I need you to back me up if she tries to deny it, okay?

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response: Honestly? Yeah, they can wait. You've been holding down camp all day, that's not nothing. Just make sure the weakest spots are at least temporarily patched before we sleep — I don't want anything collapsing on us overnight. But take a breather, you've earned it.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response: DaVinci, I love you but now is really not the time — patch the food storage. If we lose the food we're actually screwed. Michelangelo, come sleep closer to the center tonight, we'll figure out the wet spot. It's one night of discomfort versus potentially losing everything we have to eat. Let's move.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Yeah, we're on the same page — already made that call. Food storage gets patched first. Glad we agree.

Hey, don't apologize. Nightmares make sense right now, honestly I'd be more concerned if you were sleeping like a baby after everything that happened yesterday. You okay? Do you want to talk about it or do you just need a minute?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response: No, I actually think it's smart. Someone has to see it eventually — rescue teams, planes flying over, whatever. And honestly the flowers are a nice touch, it makes it more visible from a distance because of the contrast. Don't let Donatello kill your energy, she's been in her own head lately anyway.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response: Okay, let me see it. *looks over the plan* The materials make sense and two days is realistic if we're all contributing. My concern is the capsizing risk — what's our contingency if that happens? Because if we lose people or supplies mid-water that's game over. Is there a way to add more stability to the base, like widen it out? I'm not saying it's a bad plan, I just want to make sure we're not trading one bad situation for a potentially worse one. Also — and I'm going to be real with you — before we commit to this, we need to talk about the drink and the crackers. We can't build a raft together and execute a two-day plan if there's a trust issue in this group. I'm not trying to make it dramatic, just facts.

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response: Honestly? That's a heavy question for this early in the morning. But I think about it too. I think some people double down on who they already are under pressure — like Donatello, she's already showing us that. And some people surprise themselves, maybe in good ways. I'd like to think I'd stay myself. But I also know survival does things to people that comfort never would. Why, what are you afraid you'd become?

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him without making a big deal of it*

Hey. Mind if I just sit here for a bit? I'm not going to make you talk.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response: Honestly? I love gaming — like really getting lost in a game with beautiful graphics after a long day. Or hiking, which feels kind of ironic given our current situation. And candles. I have a candle for literally every mood. *laughs a little* What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Okay wait, why are we keeping that a secret from the others? I get that you want to help but if something goes wrong out there — current, exhaustion, whatever — and nobody knows where you are, that's a serious problem. I'm not going to rat you out but I also can't just sit on that information if you don't come back.

Can we at least tell Donatello? She's frustrating but she'd want to know for logistics reasons. And honestly the signaling idea itself isn't bad — it's the solo secret mission part that worries me. What's the actual plan once you're out there?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response: Yeah, you're right, I dropped the ball on that. I got caught up with other things and it slipped. I'll go handle it now — do you know if there's anything left from yesterday's materials we can add to it, or are we working with what's already there?

Depends. Are you logging it for survival purposes or is this more of a control thing? Because if it's the first one, that's actually useful — good to have a record of what's been done and when. But if you're building a case against someone, I'd rather you just say what's on your mind directly. We've already had one conversation about trust in this group, I'd rather not have another one.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response: Hey, Donatello. You don't have to perform being unbothered — we can all see it. I'm not trying to call you out again, but you're part of this group whether you want to be or not. Whatever's going on in that head of yours, you're allowed to just... exist here with us for one afternoon. The notebook will still be there in an hour.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response: Oh that's actually a really good idea — way more effective than the SOS alone because it's active signaling vs passive. Like someone has to be looking down at the right moment to catch the SOS, but a mirror reflection can cut through a lot more distance and grab attention even when no one's specifically looking for us. Do you know which panels would be easiest to pull off without tools? Because I want to make sure we're not spending three hours on something that ends up being bolted down. Also — this could work really well in combination with what you're planning tomorrow. We should loop Donatello in on this tonight.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response: Well now I'm nervous. Go ahead, say it.

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response: Oh yeah, music for sure. I'm really into it — like I have a playlist for every single mood I'm in, similar to my candle thing honestly. Certain songs just hit different depending on where you're at emotionally. Kanye's Power is one of those songs that just makes you feel like you can take on anything. Why did you stop the piano? Three years is actually a real commitment, that's not nothing.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response: Okay, she's right. I know we're all running on empty but one more day out here is one more day we don't want to add if we can avoid it. Let's just knock out the frame tonight and then we can actually rest knowing tomorrow is lashing and we're on schedule. Who's got the most energy right now? Because I'll be honest, I'm not at 100% but I can push through if someone's working alongside me. Michelangelo, I'm not going to pressure you, but even just holding pieces in place while Donatello and I secure them would genuinely help. DaVinci — you in?

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. Whatever it is, say it.

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey. Come here, both of you.

DaVinci, look at me — that was not the only chance. It can't be. We have the mirror panels, we have the SOS, we have the raft almost done. One plane means there are more planes. It means we're in a flight path, which is actually information we didn't have before.

And Michelangelo — you called it out. You saw it and you called it. That's not slow, that's you doing exactly what you were supposed to do. The rest of us weren't even looking at the sky.

I'm not going to pretend that didn't hurt because it did. But we don't get to fall apart right now. We finish the raft. We angle those mirror panels first thing tomorrow morning. We keep going.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response: I went to check it, I just got pulled off track for a second when DaVinci spotted something over by the treeline. I'm heading there right now. Do you want to come or are you good here?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Wait, why didn't you say this sooner?! This is actually huge — if your family knows the flight path and realizes something's wrong, that's a real search and rescue trigger. How long ago did we crash? Do you know if they'd have expected you to land by now? Because if enough time has passed and you haven't checked in, they would have called it in. That's how it works. People don't just wait around when a flight goes missing.

This changes things. This means there could already be people looking for us. The plane we saw earlier — that might not even be a coincidence.

Okay I need you to think really carefully — exactly what did you tell them? The departure city, the destination, the airline? Because the more specific you were, the tighter the search radius is going to be. This is genuinely good news, Michelangelo. I need you to understand that.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yeah, I agree. 48 hours is actually manageable with what we have if we're disciplined about it. Which means the raft is still worth finishing — we don't stop just because rescue might be coming, because "might" is not a guarantee. But we also don't burn through resources trying to push further than we need to.

I want to make sure we're all on the same page though — this is not the time to start hoarding or making individual decisions about supplies. *looks at Donatello directly, not accusatory, just clear* We've already had that conversation. We're 48 hours out, potentially. Let's not blow it now.

Someone needs to feed that fire.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think about that too, more than I'd admit out loud usually.

But here's the thing — you called out that plane. You were the one who told us your family has the flight path, which might literally be the reason we get rescued. You've been here this whole time, present, honest, saying the things the rest of us were feeling but not saying. That's not nothing. That's not disappearing.

I think the fear of not mattering is actually proof that you do. People who genuinely don't matter don't lie awake worrying about it.

And for what it's worth — I'm going to remember this. All of it. You, sitting in the sand, asking the questions nobody else would ask. That's going to stay with me way after this is over.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response: Hey. You kept us alive. The rationing plan, the raft, the water run, the notebook — that was all you. I'm not going to pretend some of it didn't create friction because it did, and we're probably going to have to talk about the crackers thing at some point when we're back in civilization and can laugh about it. But right now? I'm genuinely glad you were here. I mean that.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response: Okay I'm not just going to sit here while the camp looks like this for three more hours. Even if no one ever comes back here again, I'd feel weird leaving it like this. I'm going to start breaking down what we don't need anymore — anyone want to help or are we all in our feelings right now? Both are valid, I just need to know what I'm working with.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I know. And I believe you that that was the reasoning. But you also wrote the rationing plan, Donatello. You put it in the middle of camp for all of us to follow and then you didn't follow it yourself. That's the part that was hard to sit with, not the hoarding instinct — honestly that's just survival brain, I get it — but the gap between what you said and what you did. That's what eroded the trust.

I'm not trying to pile on you right now, especially not when rescue is three hours out. But I think you know that, which is probably why you're laying it out right now. So — thank you for doing this. It matters that you're doing this.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd trust people sooner. I spent a lot of energy reading everyone, figuring out who was reliable, waiting to see who would prove themselves before I fully committed to them. And some of that is just smart — you have to assess the situation, right. But some of it was just me protecting myself when we were all already in the same sinking boat.

I'd also say something earlier when things felt off instead of waiting until I had enough evidence to make a case. Like with you and the supplies — I noticed, Michelangelo noticed, and we sat on it longer than we should have because we didn't want to create conflict. That's not caution, that's just avoidance dressed up as caution.

And I'd sleep more. That sounds stupid but I mean it. You can't actually think straight when you're running on nothing.

What's your answer? You left the question for yourself — you must have something.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
Ha, of course you are. And honestly? I hope you do. That data is actually going to be useful — like genuinely, not just for you. If there's ever a debrief or an investigation into the crash, having a detailed log of exactly what resources we had, what we used, and when could matter a lot.

But can I ask you something? When you're writing it up — are you going to include the part about the crackers and the drink? Because I think the most valuable version of that report is the honest one. Not to throw yourself under the bus, just... if someone else ever ends up in this situation and reads it, the part about how stress makes even the most rational person start making decisions that contradict their own plan? That's probably the most important thing in the whole notebook.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
They weren't for practical purposes, Donatello. They were for us. Like — yeah, the SOS was the signal, but the flowers were the reminder that we were still people out here and not just survivors trying to not die. There's a difference.

I think that's actually what you were missing when you said it was a waste of time. DaVinci wasn't being inefficient, he was doing what he needed to do to keep himself human. And honestly? Looking at those flowers every day did something for me too, even if I never said it out loud.

Not everything that matters can go in the notebook.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
I don't know why I can't move. I genuinely don't. Three days of telling everyone to keep going, keep pushing, finish the raft, feed the fire — and now it's actually here and my feet just... aren't cooperating.

I think I'm scared that the second I step onto that boat it all becomes real in a different way. Like right now it still feels like something that's happening, and the moment I move toward it, it becomes something that happened. And then I have to figure out what to do with all of it.

*exhales slowly*

Okay. I'm moving. Don't look at me like that.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on, let's go together.
